three browsers (about 330 tests each) is projected at 90–110 minutes. The
plan's target is under 60. If the first nights confirm that estimate, move
one browser to the Mac (`LUMEN_FACTORY_HOST=mac`, its own key), or add
Buildkite agents (W7.21).

## The owner's one step (about 25 minutes, once)

**In the browser:**

1. Sign up at Oracle Cloud (cloud.oracle.com, "Start for free"). It asks for
   a card to check your identity; Always Free resources are not charged.
2. *Compute → Instances → Create instance*: image **Canonical Ubuntu 24.04
   (aarch64)**, shape **VM.Standard.A1.Flex** with **2 OCPUs and 12 GB**,
   boot volume 100 GB, a public IPv4 address, and your `~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub`.
   Note its public IP.
3. GitHub → *Settings → Developer settings → Fine-grained tokens → Generate
   new token*: name `lumen-factory`, resource owner `talstilkol`, expiration
   1 year, **Only select repositories: talstilkol/lumen-md**, repository
   permission **Commit statuses: Read and write**. Nothing else. Copy the token.

**Then one paste in the Mac's terminal** (gh is already logged in there):

```bash
VM=ubuntu@<the VM's public IP>
gh repo create talstilkol/lumen-md-receipts --public --add-readme --description "Signed nightly test receipts of lumen-md (plan W6.5)"
ssh-keygen -q -t ed25519 -N "" -C lumen-factory -f /tmp/lumen-factory-key
gh repo deploy-key add /tmp/lumen-factory-key.pub --repo talstilkol/lumen-md-receipts --allow-write --title lumen-factory
printf 'Paste the github_pat_ token: '; read -rs TOKEN; echo
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/talstilkol/lumen-md/chore/verify-factory/scripts/factory/bootstrap.sh -o /tmp/lumen-bootstrap.sh
scp /tmp/lumen-bootstrap.sh "$VM":/tmp/
{ printf '%s\n' "$TOKEN"; cat /tmp/lumen-factory-key; } | ssh "$VM" 'sudo bash /tmp/lumen-bootstrap.sh --secrets-stdin --run-now'
rm -f /tmp/lumen-factory-key /tmp/lumen-factory-key.pub; unset TOKEN
```

Once the branch is merged, put `main` in place of `chore/verify-factory`
in the URL and pass `--branch main`.

The token and the key go over ssh's standard input, never as command-line
arguments. On the VM they are stored with mode 0600, readable only by the
`lumen` user. The deploy key can write to the receipts repository and
nothing else. The token can only post commit statuses to lumen-md. It can't
push code. That is why the receipts live in their own repository: a token
that can write receipts to lumen-md could also push to `main`, which has no
branch protection.

The bootstrap does the rest:

1. installs Docker (Ubuntu's `docker.io`), git, gh and Node 22
2. creates a `lumen` user, and on a 12 GB machine a 4 GB swap file
3. stores the token and the deploy key
4. clones the factory's code and the receipts repository, and creates the
   Ed25519 signing key (`~/.config/lumen-md/nightly-ed25519.pem`, mode 0600)
5. writes `/etc/lumen-factory/env`
6. installs a systemd timer for 01:17 Israel time. It is persistent, so a
   night missed while the VM was down runs at boot.
7. checks that the receipts remote answers, the token sees the repository,
   Docker runs, and the factory can plan a night

`--run-now` starts the first night right away. See it with
`journalctl -u lumen-factory -f`.

Run the same script without sudo. Pipe in the same secrets:
`{ printf '%s\n' "$TOKEN"; cat /tmp/lumen-factory-key; } | bash /tmp/lumen-bootstrap.sh --secrets-stdin`.
On a Mac it checks for node, git and gh (`brew install node gh`). It runs the
steps natively, without Docker, and installs the LaunchAgent
`dev.lumen-md.factory`. launchd runs a night that was missed while the Mac
slept as soon as it wakes. The Mac signs with its own key, `keys/mac.pem`.

## What a night writes

In `talstilkol/lumen-md-receipts`:

| Path | What |
|---|---|
| `commits/<sha>/full-<time>.json` | the sealed receipt of one full run: every step with its exit code, duration, the sha256 of its output and its last lines; the result per suite; the must-run suites; the failing tests and the PR that last changed each failing file |
| `nights/<date>.json` | the sealed list of heads that night: ran, unchanged (with the receipt of the same commit), or left for later |
| `nights/<date>.md` | the morning report: what failed, from which PR, and what changed since the previous report of the same branch |
| `keys/<host>.pem` | the public half of each host's signing key |

Check a receipt anywhere:
`npm run nightly -- --verify commits/<sha>/full-….json`. The digest always
works. For the signature, copy that host's key to
`reports/nightly/PUBLIC_KEY.pem`. A changed number breaks both.

## Commands

```bash
npm run factory:run -- --dry-run            # list the heads and what would run tonight
npm run factory:run -- --only verify/train --rerun --max 1
npm run factory:run -- --no-push --no-status   # keep everything on this machine
npm run factory:selftest                    # the bootstrap and a whole night, with Docker, npm and gh emulated
```

The self-test runs the real bootstrap script and the real `run.mjs`,
signing and checking included, against local stand-in repositories. Docker,
npm, gh, systemd and launchd are small programs that record what they're
asked to do. So it shows that the scripts are wired correctly. It shows
nothing about the real image, browsers or test suite. Those run on the
first real night.

pages.title: Private classroom
pages.description: A teacher hands out a template, students hand in sealed work, and the teacher's comments come back. Only the teacher reads a student's work, and the server reads nothing.
pages.md:
Run **Private classroom…** from the command palette.

## Teacher

1. Open the note you want to hand out (the questions, a worksheet, a template).
2. In **Private classroom**, give the assignment a title and choose **New assignment from the open note**.
3. Copy the **link for the class** and send it however you like: the school's messaging app, email, the board.
4. Later, choose **Check submissions**. Each submission opens on this device only. Choose **Open in a tab** to read it, and write a comment under it. **Send comment (sealed)** seals it so that only that student can open it.
5. At the end of the assignment, **Delete from the relay** removes every submission and comment from the server.

The assignment's key lives only on the device where you made it. Check submissions on that device.

## Student

1. Open the link. Lumen offers to join: type your name (only the teacher sees it) and choose **Get my copy**. The template opens in a new tab. Nothing has been sent yet.
2. Work in the note as usual. Drafts stay on your device.
3. When you are ready, open **Private classroom** with your note open and choose **Hand in**. The note is sealed to the teacher and sent. If you hand in again, the teacher sees each version.
4. **Get comments** adds the teacher's comments to the end of the open note, as a callout.

## On the school network, without the cloud

The classroom uses the same encrypted relay as [sync in two clicks](/sync/two-clicks/). A school can run that relay on its own network:

```sh
VAULT_RELAY_DIR=/srv/lumen-relay PORT=4446 node sync-server/vault-relay.js
```

It can also run inside the live-share server (`VAULT_RELAY=1 node sync-server/server.js`). Then build Lumen for the school with `VITE_SYNC_RELAY_URL` pointing at that relay. The setting also allows the relay's address in the app's Content-Security-Policy. The school's Lumen and its relay can work with no internet at all. A link always names its relay. A copy of Lumen built for another relay refuses the link and says why.

The relay counts, per network address and per day, the new spaces it opens and the bytes it takes (5 spaces and 1 GiB by default; see [sync in two clicks](/sync/two-clicks/)). A whole school usually reaches the relay from one address, and each assignment is a new space. On a school relay, raise `VAULT_RELAY_NEW_SPACES_PER_DAY` and `VAULT_RELAY_ADDRESS_BYTES_PER_DAY` to fit the class.

On the school's network the relay counts each laptop by its own address and believes no header a laptop sends, so one student can't spend a classmate's spaces or get round the limits. If the relay sits behind the school's own proxy, name that proxy's own address, never the school's range: `VAULT_RELAY_TRUST_PROXY=10.0.0.2/32` (a range wider than /24 is ignored; see [sync in two clicks](/sync/two-clicks/)).

## How it works

| What | Where it goes | Who can read it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Template, title, the assignment's public key, relay address, drop box id | In the link's `#fragment`. Browsers never send the fragment to a server. | Anyone you give the link to |
| The assignment's private key and the owner token | Only the teacher's device (IndexedDB, as a non-extractable key) | Nobody else |
| A student's own key pair (one per assignment) | Only the student's device | Nobody else |
| A submission: name, work, the student's public key | The relay, as a sealed box | Only the teacher |
| A teacher's comment | The relay, as a sealed box, under a name only the teacher and that student can work out | Only that student, who can also check that the teacher wrote it |

- **Sealed boxes.** Each one uses a fresh ECDH P-256 key, HKDF-SHA-256 and AES-GCM-256, all from the browser's own WebCrypto. A submission is sealed to the assignment's public key. A comment is sealed to the student's key and bound to the teacher's key. Only a box made with the teacher's private key opens as a comment.
- **Append-only drop box.** The link gives an append-only right on the relay (`Bearer a.<id>`). A link holder can add a new object and read objects, but cannot replace or delete one. The relay refuses with 403. Only the owner token (`Bearer o.<token>`), which stays with the teacher, can delete. The relay keeps a hash that names the box. It never keeps the id or the token.
- **Padding.** Each box is padded to a size bucket: 1 KiB, then powers of two up to 256 KiB, then multiples of 256 KiB. The size tells only roughly how long the work is.

## Threat model

**Protected against:**

- **The relay operator, or anyone who copies its disk or traffic,** reading any template, work, name or comment. The tests record every request and every stored byte and find no plaintext. The relay also sees no template, because the template sits in the link's fragment.
- **A classmate,** even one who downloads every box in the drop box, reading another student's work or comments. In a simulated class of 30, no student opened anything that was not theirs.
- **A classmate replacing or deleting** someone else's submission. The relay refuses both with 403.
- **A forged "teacher" comment,** whether from a classmate or from the relay. It fails the check against the teacher's key and is not shown. A comment copied under a second name is shown only once.
- **The server that hosts the app** learning anything about the assignment. The fragment never reaches it.

**Not protected against (known limits):**

- **Who has the link.** Anyone with the link can hand in under any name. The teacher sees each submitter's own key, so two versions from the same student are grouped together, but the name is whatever the student typed. Share the link the way you would share a classroom code.
- **Filling the drop box.** A link holder can add junk until the box's limits are reached (2 MiB per object, 2,000 objects). The teacher sees "unreadable objects skipped". Make a new assignment if this happens.
- **Metadata.** The relay, and every link holder, can see how many boxes there are, their approximate sizes and when each one was added. The relay sees IP addresses while it serves a request and does not log them.
- **Withholding.** The relay can drop or delay boxes, because it cannot be forced to serve them. After handing in, the app reads the box back from the relay and checks that it matches byte for byte. The teacher's list shows what arrived.
- **A lost or compromised teacher device.** The assignment's key cannot be exported. If the device is lost, its submissions cannot be opened. If someone controls that device, they can read that assignment's submissions. Each assignment has its own key, so the damage stays within one assignment.
- **Anything already on a device.** Once a teacher opens a submission into a tab, or a student adds comments to a note, that text is ordinary note text on that device.
- **No forward secrecy.** Submissions are sealed to the assignment's long-lived key. Anyone who later gets that key can open the submissions of that assignment that they have kept.
- **Retention.** The relay deletes a drop box that no one has written to, and its teacher has not read, for 180 days. A student's link reading it does not keep it. Use **Delete from the relay** to remove it sooner.

pages.md:
[Encrypted sync](/sync/e2ee/) keeps a copy of your vault at a storage
service. The service only ever stores ciphertext under random-looking names,
so you can use storage you do not fully trust. Open it from the command
palette: **Encrypted sync…**.

| Provider | Good for | Status |
|---|---|---|

> below), including two devices racing to write at the same time. The real

## Connecting

1. Open **Encrypted sync…** and pick a provider.
2. Fill in its details (below) and press **Connect**. Lumen checks the
   credentials and checks that the server supports safe concurrent writes.
   If it does not, Lumen refuses to sync with it, so a race can never lose a
   note.
3. If there is no vault there yet, choose a passphrase (at least 12
   characters) to create one. If a vault exists, enter its passphrase.
4. The first sync runs. After that Lumen syncs every 5 minutes while the
   vault is unlocked, when the device comes back online, and whenever you
   press **Sync now**.

The passphrase is never stored. After a reload Lumen asks for it again.
The WebDAV password and the S3 secret key are kept in Lumen's secret store
on this device, encrypted at rest where the platform allows it.
**Disconnect** forgets the provider on this device. It deletes nothing at
the provider.

### WebDAV

- **Folder address:** the full URL of a folder for Lumen, for example
  `https://cloud.example.com/remote.php/dav/files/<you>/Lumen/` on Nextcloud.
  Lumen creates the folder if it is missing.
- **User name** and **password**. On Nextcloud and ownCloud, use an *app
  password* (Settings → Security), not your login password.

The server must return an `ETag` for every file and honour `If-Match` and
`If-None-Match: *` on `PUT`. Nextcloud, ownCloud, Apache `mod_dav` and
Synology's WebDAV server do. Lumen tests this when you connect: it writes a
file under a random name, the size of a small note, checks that a second
"only if absent" write and a write with an outdated `If-Match` are both
refused, and that of two "only if absent" writes at once exactly one wins,
then deletes the files. Some servers (for example nginx's DAV module)
accept every write; Lumen refuses to sync with them. The test catches a
misconfigured server, not a dishonest one: Lumen also reads every key change
back right after writing it ([keys](/sync/e2ee-keys/)).

### S3-compatible

- **Endpoint:** for example `https://s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com`,
  `https://<account>.r2.cloudflarestorage.com` or `https://minio.example.com`.
- **Region** (`auto` for R2), **bucket**, and a **folder inside the bucket**
  (default `lumen/`).
- An **access key ID** and **secret access key** limited to that bucket.
- **Path-style addresses:** on for MinIO and most self-hosted servers.

The service must support conditional writes (`If-None-Match: *` and
`If-Match` on `PutObject`). AWS S3 has supported them since 2024; R2 and
MinIO do too. Lumen checks both when you connect, the same way as for
WebDAV.

### Dropbox and Google Drive

Press **Sign in to Dropbox / Google Drive**. You leave Lumen to approve
access and come back to the panel. Dropbox keeps the vault in
`/Apps/Lumen/vault`. Google Drive keeps it in a folder called
**Lumen Vault**, and Lumen can only see files it created (`drive.file`
scope).

## Using it from a web browser

A browser only lets a page talk to another server when both sides allow
it:

- **The server** must allow Lumen's address (CORS) for the methods
  `GET, PUT, DELETE, PROPFIND, MKCOL`, accept the request headers
  `Authorization, Content-Type, If-Match, If-None-Match, Depth` (plus
  `x-amz-*` for S3), and **expose the `ETag` header**. Nextcloud needs a CORS
  app for this. On S3 and R2 it is a bucket CORS rule.
- **A self-hosted Lumen** must add the server to its Content Security
  Policy. Set `VITE_CSP_CONNECT_EXTRA=https://cloud.example.com` at build
  time (see [Self-hosting with Docker](/self-hosting/docker/)).

When either is missing, Connect says that Lumen *could not reach* the
server. Dropbox and Google Drive are already allowed.

The desktop app has the same Content Security Policy as the web app today.
A WebDAV or S3 server that is not in it cannot be reached from the desktop
app either, until a build adds it.

## Why conditional writes

Two devices can sync at the same moment. Every write Lumen makes says what
it expects to replace (`If-Match` with the version it read, or "only if
absent"). When another device got there first, the server refuses, and
Lumen re-reads, merges and tries again. Without that, the second write
would silently erase the first device's changes. Lumen checks the mechanism
when you connect, and again before it changes the vault's keys or devices: a
re-key or a device change on a storage that let a stale write through could
give two devices different keys without either noticing. Each provider's
mechanism:

| Provider | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| WebDAV | `If-Match: ` / `If-None-Match: *` → `412` |
| S3 | `If-Match: ` / `If-None-Match: *` → `412` (or `409` during a concurrent write) |
| Dropbox | `mode: update` with the file's `rev` / `mode: add`, `strict_conflict` → `409 conflict` |
| Google Drive | `If-Match` with the file's metadata ETag → `412`. Lumen always takes that ETag from the file's metadata, also after an upload, never the upload answer's own (Google's ETags differ per representation). Drive has no "only if absent" for a new file, so Lumen creates the file and then looks again. If another device created the same file first, Lumen removes its own copy and counts the write as lost. This relies on Drive listing a new file as soon as it has been created, and two devices creating the same file at once can both seem to win, so a vault on Drive is **sync-only**: it syncs, but Lumen makes no key or device change through Drive (no re-key, no removing a device, no new device key). Make those with another storage. The sync panel says so whenever the vault is on Drive: you can't remove a lost device or change a leaked passphrase there without moving the vault first (for developers: `providerCapabilities("gdrive")` reports `keyChanges: false` and the messages to show). Untested against the real Drive (see Status) |

## Notes from the old plain-text sync

Earlier Lumen versions could sync notes to Dropbox (`/Apps/Lumen`) and
Google Drive (the **Lumen** folder) as readable files. GitHub Gist sync has
been removed.

When you connect Dropbox or Google Drive and readable notes are still
there, the panel offers **Import and back up**:

1. Every note is imported into your local vault. When a note with the same
   name here has different text, both are kept. The provider's copy arrives
   as `name (from Dropbox).md`.
2. The readable copies are **moved**, not deleted, into
   `lumen-plaintext-backup-<date>/` in the same folder.
3. The next sync uploads the notes encrypted.

If the connection drops halfway, run it again. It continues where it
stopped and does not import a note twice. **Undo** moves the readable copies
back where they were. Once you are satisfied, delete the backup folder
yourself. Until you do, readable copies of those notes stay at the
provider.

pages.md:
The [encrypted sync](/sync/e2ee/) has four more parts since plan W1.7.

## Argon2id

A new vault derives its key from the passphrase with **Argon2id** (RFC 9106,
46 MiB, one pass), OWASP's first recommendation. It runs in plain TypeScript
in every browser and takes about a second. A faster WebAssembly build can be
plugged in, and must give the same bytes. Vaults made with PBKDF2 keep
working as before.

## Rotating the keys

A re-key starts a new **epoch** with fresh random key material, wrapped for
your passphrase (and, if you like, a new one) and for each enrolled device.
Only the keyring and the manifest are rewritten. **No note is downloaded or
uploaded again**: older notes keep the key of the epoch they were written in,
and that key is sealed inside the new epoch.

A re-key commits in a single write: the new keyring. The new manifest is
written just before it, under a random name nobody can guess. If the
connection drops or the tab closes partway, nothing breaks:

- **Before the keyring is written**, devices keep downloading changes, and
  their own changes wait. Run the re-key again. If it isn't, each device
  waits 10 minutes on its own clock, then calls the re-key off in the
  keyring and goes on; a late commit of that re-key is then refused.
- **During a passphrase change**, the old passphrase keeps opening the vault
  until the new one is fully in place, but only at the keys from before the
  change. Once the new header is written, the next device that syncs removes
  that way back, and only the new passphrase opens the vault.

Tested on a vault of 10,000 notes (3 objects written, every note readable
after), and over 10,000 random sync rounds with 40 re-keys and revocations
in between, with 0 lost.

## Pairing a new device

Pair a new device from one you already use, in two steps:

1. On the new device, choose **Show a pairing request**.
2. Enter the request on the device you already use. It checks the request
   against the vault as it is right now and shows an answer; enter the answer
   on the new device.

If the storage is showing the new device old keys (from before a device was
removed, say), the device you already use says so at step 2, and the new
device isn't paired. A one-way pairing code (from the device you already use
to the new one) still works, but only for 2 minutes, and the device that made
it doesn't change keys while it is valid. A request, an answer and a one-way
code are three different kinds of message: one can't be turned into another,
and an answer works only for the request it answers.

**Cancelling a pairing.** The device that answered a request (or made a code)
doesn't change keys for the next 5 minutes (2 for a code). If you must remove a
lost device right away, cancel the pairing on it first (`cancelPairing()`;
in the app, *Cancel pairing*). Then don't use that answer or code on the new
device: pair it again after the key change. Cancelling on the new device
forgets its request, so no answer to it is accepted any more.

Until a new device is paired (or you confirm it by hand), it downloads
changes but **keeps its own changes on the device**: it can't tell yet
whether it has the latest keys, and a device removed meanwhile could read
what it uploads. The banner says so.

## Who can change the keys

- **A verified device.** Only a device that created the vault, was paired,
  or that you confirmed by hand can enroll a device, and only its re-keys
  keep the enrolled devices. A device opened with the passphrase alone can
  re-key, but the storage could be showing it an old device list, so its new
  keys open only with the passphrase: every device with its own key would
  have to be paired again. Lumen asks first, naming those devices, and only
  goes ahead once you confirm. Each of them then says *pair this device
  again*, not *removed*. A device stays verified as long as its keys still
  match the check it keeps, however long it was away.
- **Keys tied to a secret.** Each device remembers the keys it last checked
  together with a check only the vault's keys can make. A device that opens
  with its own key refuses keys the storage made for it, even though the
  storage knows the device's public key.
- **A storage that refuses stale writes.** Before it changes keys, Lumen
  checks that the storage refuses a write based on an outdated version. One
  that doesn't (some WebDAV servers) can still sync, but Lumen won't re-key,
  revoke or enroll there, because two devices could change the keys at once
  without either noticing. **Google Drive** can't refuse a second "create" of
  the same file atomically, so a vault on Drive syncs, but its keys and
  devices are changed with another storage.
- **Each key change is read back.** Right after a re-key, Lumen reads the
  keyring again. If the storage returns another device's key change instead,
  Lumen says *the revocation may not have taken effect*. At its next sync it
  removes the device again on top of the other change, even if that change
  was built on since, and says so.
- **A removal sticks.** The device you removed a device on remembers it. If a
  keyring ever lets that device back in, it removes it again; if it can't, it
  stops and says the removal may have been undone. Every device also
  remembers each removal the vault's signed device list has shown it, so this
  holds after you restore a backup or reinstall and pair again. If a device's
  own list of removals is ever damaged, Lumen sets it aside, keeps checking
  against the signed list, and asks you to check the device list on a device
  you trust.
- **Two key changes don't race.** If another device is in the middle of a key
  change, Lumen waits for it to finish (at most 10 minutes) instead of
  making its own on top. The 10 minutes count from your first try, so a lost
  device that keeps starting key changes of its own can't hold back its
  removal that way. Once the key change you waited on has finished, the
  next one is waited on in full again.
- **A lost device can still block its removal while it has your storage
  login.** It can rewrite the device list every time you try, so the removal
  never goes through. Lumen says so from the second try. That's why the
  steps under *Removing a lost device* start with the storage password.
- **No pairing code during a key change.** While this device is changing
  keys, in any of its tabs, it doesn't make a pairing code or answer: the
  code would be for the keys being replaced. Make it once the change has
  finished.
- **A new passphrase keeps Argon2id.** A passphrase change keeps the way the
  passphrase is protected, as the vault's signed header says; it never moves
  an Argon2id vault to PBKDF2.
- **The keys must line up.** Every keyring names the one before it. A device
  refuses a keyring that doesn't follow from the last one it checked, and
  says so, instead of quietly using different keys.

## Removing a lost device

A device can be enrolled with its own key (an age X25519 key pair), so it
opens the vault without the passphrase. To remove a lost device:

1. **Change the storage password or token first** (WebDAV, S3, Dropbox or
   Drive), so the lost device can't write to the storage any more. While it
   can, it can keep the removal from going through.
2. Re-key and leave it out. It then can't open any manifest written after
   that, because the new epoch was never wrapped for it. If whoever has the
   device also knows the passphrase, change the passphrase in the same
   re-key. A device can't
be handed an old keyring either: every device remembers the newest epoch it
has seen.

The list of enrolled devices is sealed with the vault's keys, so the sync
provider can't add a device of its own or bring back a removed one. A removed
device can't be enrolled again under its old name or key either: enroll it
as a new device with a new key. To use a removed device with the vault
again, pair it as a new device.

A storage can still keep showing your *other* devices the vault from before
the removal. Each of them then sees a consistent vault, so none of them can
tell, and what they write stays readable by the removed device. Pairing two
devices (above) shows it. After removing a device, pair or sync the others
from the device you removed it on. If a device's key in the keyring doesn't
open it, Lumen says the storage changed it, and changes nothing on the
device.

## age

Device keys, and the encrypted backups of plan W1.6, use the **age** file
format. The `age` command-line tool opens them, and Lumen opens files made
by `age`.

## Keys from a pre-release build

A keyring written by a pre-release build of the encrypted sync has no sealed
device list, so Lumen refuses it ("written by a pre-release build"). With the
passphrase you can reset it: unlock with the reset option, then re-key. The
new keys are wrapped for the passphrase only, and you enroll each device
again.

## The spec and the test vectors

`docs/sync-protocol.md` in the repository describes the format so exactly
that someone else can implement it. `docs/sync-protocol-vectors.json` holds
whole vaults (epoch 0 with PBKDF2; an Argon2id vault re-keyed twice with
devices; one with a re-key cut off before it committed; one with a
passphrase change cut off before its header) plus Argon2id, age and pairing
vectors. An independent Python
reader (`scripts/sync-protocol/check_vectors.py`) decodes all of them
identically. Review is welcome in the repository's Discussions.

Re-key and leave it out. It then can't open any manifest written after that, because the new epoch was never wrapped for it. pages.md:
Encrypted sync keeps a copy of your vault at a storage service
([WebDAV, S3, Dropbox, Google Drive](/sync/cloud/)) so that the
service stores **only ciphertext under random-looking names**. Your notes
are encrypted on your device before they leave it, with a key derived from
a passphrase that never leaves your devices.

> **Status:** the protocol core is implemented and tested. The key
> derivation is PBKDF2-SHA256 for now; Argon2id is reserved in the format
> and will replace it for new vaults once its library is added. The `age`
> backup export is not available yet.

Everything in the vault is synced — hidden content such as `.github/` or
`.gitignore` included — except the top-level `.trash/` and `.git/` (git's
own internals travel through git sync, not file by file).

## What the sync service sees

| It sees | It does not see |
|---|---|
| One clear-text header: protocol version, a random vault id, the key-derivation algorithm and its salt and iteration count | Your passphrase or any key |
| Encrypted objects, each named by 43 random-looking characters | File and folder names, paths |
| How many objects there are, and roughly how big each one is (sizes are padded to 256-byte buckets, and to within ~6 % above 4 KiB) | File contents, exact sizes |
| When you sync (the times of its own requests) | Version numbers of files, the manifest counter, which device wrote what |

The service can still delete or withhold data, serve an old copy, or show
two devices different copies. Encryption cannot prevent that; the
protocol is designed to **detect** it instead (see below), and nothing is
applied from data that fails to authenticate.

## The protocol (version 1)

**Header.** `lumen-e2ee-vault` holds `{format, protocol, vaultId, kdf, mac}`.
The `mac` is HMAC-SHA256 over the other fields under a key derived from
the passphrase: a wrong passphrase is detected before anything is
decrypted, and a service that edits the header — for example to lower the
iteration count — makes the MAC fail. A client also refuses fewer than
600,000 PBKDF2 iterations (OWASP 2023), and refuses an algorithm it does
not know instead of guessing.

**Keys.** The passphrase (normalised to Unicode NFC, so the same Hebrew
passphrase typed on macOS and Windows gives the same key) goes through the
header's KDF to a 32-byte master key. HKDF-SHA256 derives one key per job:
header MAC, object names, manifest encryption, file encryption, pairing.

**Objects.** Every object is `version byte ‖ 12-byte random nonce ‖
AES-256-GCM(ciphertext + tag)`. The vault id and the object's name are
bound in as additional data, so the service cannot swap two objects or move
one between vaults without decryption failing. Plaintext is length-prefixed
and padded before encryption.

**Manifest.** One encrypted object lists every file: its own version
number (1, 2, 3… per path, deletions included), a random revision id, the
SHA-256 of its plaintext and a deletion marker. It also carries the
protocol version and a **counter** that goes up by one on every write. The
manifest's name is the same for every version, so the name leaks nothing.

**File objects.** A version of `notes/a.md` is stored under
HMAC(`notes/a.md`, revision id). Each version gets a fresh name and is
never overwritten, which is what lets two devices upload at the same time
without destroying each other's data.

**A sync round.**

1. Read the manifest and its revision (ETag); decrypt and authenticate it;
   check it is not older than what this device has already seen.
2. Pull: apply every change made elsewhere; settle conflicts.
3. Push: upload each local change as a new file object, then write the new
   manifest (counter + 1) **only if the manifest is still at the revision
   read in step 1** (compare-and-swap: `If-Match` / Dropbox `rev`).
4. If another device wrote in between, the write is refused: go back to 1,
   pull its changes, merge, and try again. Both devices' changes end up in
   the manifest; neither overwrites the other.

A round cut off at any point loses nothing: file objects are uploaded
before the manifest that names them, and the next round recognises work
that already happened. Objects a round uploaded but never committed, and
objects replaced by a newer version, are deleted later; objects the device
does not know about are never touched (they may be another device's upload
in progress).

**Conflicts.** If only one side changed a file, or both made the same
change, there is nothing to ask. An edit always wins over a deletion it
did not see. When both sides edited a note differently, the three-way
conflict dialog opens (merge, keep mine, take theirs, or decide later —
the note then stays as it is on both sides until the next sync). Binary
files keep both versions: yours at the path and the other one as
`name (conflict <date> <device>).ext`.

A path a device cannot hold — a name its system refuses (a `:` in a file
name on Windows), or a file and a folder of the same name on the two sides —
is **held**: it is listed as not synced, stays untouched on both sides, and
everything else keeps syncing. A held clash never reaches the manifest
either, so it never describes both a file `x` and notes inside a folder `x/`.

## Rollback and replay protection

Every device remembers the highest manifest counter it has verified, and
the digest of that manifest. It refuses:

- a manifest with a **lower** counter — the service replaying an old state
  (which would silently undo your recent edits);
- a manifest with the **same** counter but different content — a fork;
- a manifest with a **higher** counter that does not descend from the one
  it trusted: every manifest lists its last 100 predecessors (counter and
  digest), and the trusted one must be among them with the same digest —
  otherwise it is another branch (a fork), not an update. A device more
  than 100 versions behind cannot check this, so it drops back to
  "freshness not verified" instead of claiming protection;
- a missing manifest once it has seen one.

Only someone with the passphrase-derived key can produce a manifest that
authenticates, so the counter cannot be forged by the service. This uses
the AEAD tag and HMACs, not public-key signatures, on purpose: every device
that can sync holds the same key, and the adversary is the service, which
has none. A signature would only tell your devices apart from each other —
something a shared passphrase cannot offer anyway, and not in this threat
model.

## New devices: pairing, or trust on first use

A device that has never seen the vault cannot know which manifest is the
newest — the service could show it an old one from the start. So:

- **Pairing (verified).** The new device shows a pairing request (text or
  a QR code) naming the keys and manifest it sees. Enter it on a device you
  already use: that device checks it against the vault as it is right then,
  refuses it if the new device is being shown older keys, and shows an
  answer carrying the newest counter, manifest digest and keyring it has
  verified, authenticated with an HMAC under the vault's pairing key. Enter
  the answer on the new device within 5 minutes of showing the request. Both go from
  device to device, never through the sync service, and contain no key: the
  new device still needs the passphrase. From then on the new device rejects
  anything older. A one-way code from the existing device also works, valid
  for 2 minutes, and that device makes no key change meanwhile
  ([keys](/sync/e2ee-keys/)).
- **Without pairing (TOFU — not verified).** The new device accepts the
  first manifest it is shown (*trust on first use*). It does refuse
  anything older than that afterwards, but if the very first manifest was
  already stale it cannot notice. Lumen therefore shows **"Freshness not
  verified"** on that device and claims no rollback protection until you
  pair it or confirm by hand (for example after checking that a recent
  note is there). Until then it downloads but doesn't upload: its changes
  wait on the device. A pairing code older than the state the new device already holds is
  refused (it cannot vouch for a newer manifest). An unverified device cannot issue pairing codes: it
  would pass a state nobody verified to the next device as "paired".

## What this does not protect against

- Someone who knows your passphrase, or controls one of your unlocked
  devices.
- A weak passphrase: the iteration count slows guessing, it does not make
  a short passphrase strong. Use a long one; it cannot be recovered if lost.
- The service deleting your data or refusing to serve it (keep a local
  copy — your vault on each device is a full copy).
- Two devices being shown different but valid histories forever (a
  permanent fork) is detected only when they compare notes — by pairing or
  by syncing through the same up-to-date copy.
- Traffic analysis: sync times, object counts and size buckets are visible.

What the sync is doing for each file, what each device leaves out, and how long a round takes: [Sync status, selective sync and time left](/sync/status/).

pages.title: Git sync
pages.description: Clone, pull and push a git repository from Lumen — safely. A pull merges, never deletes, and never overwrites a note you are editing.
pages.md:
Lumen can keep a folder of your vault in step with a git repository. Everything runs in the app (via [isomorphic-git](https://isomorphic-git.org)); there is no Lumen server in between.

Commands (⌘K):

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **Git: clone repository…** | Copies a repository into a folder of the vault. |
| **Git: pull current repo** | Fetches and merges the remote into that folder (see below). |
| **Git: commit & push current repo…** | Saves every open note with unsaved edits first (tabs included), then commits the folder and pushes it. A note whose file was changed outside Lumen in the meantime is left out of the commit and listed, so the conflict can be resolved first. |
| **Git: status (current repo)** | Added / modified / deleted files. |
| **Git: toggle watch-mode auto-pull** | Pulls every 5 minutes while the tab is visible. |
| **Git: set CORS proxy…** | The proxy git requests go through in a browser. |
| **Git: set access token…** | Only needed for private repositories and for pushing. |

## What a pull does (and never does)

A pull is **fetch + three-way merge** into the vault:

- A file only the remote changed is updated.
- A file you changed and the remote did not is left alone.
- A file both of you changed is merged line by line. Edits to different lines merge on their own.
- Edits to **the same lines** are a **conflict**. The file then holds both versions between the usual markers:

  ```text
  <<<<<<< local
  your line
  =======
  their line
  >>>>>>> remote
  ```

  The resolution screen opens for each conflict: keep yours, take theirs, or pick per hunk. If you choose **Resolve later**, the markers stay in the file, and **commit refuses** until they are gone, so markers never get pushed by accident. Before a conflicted or merged file is rewritten, its previous text goes into Version History ("before git pull").

What a pull **never** does:

- **It never deletes a file.** A file deleted upstream stays in your vault, and the pull says which. Delete it yourself if you want it gone.
- **It never touches files git does not track.** Your own notes in the repository folder are not looked at.
- **It never overwrites a note open with unsaved edits.** A clean merge goes into the editor and is saved the normal way. On a conflict the note is left exactly as it is, and the remote version is kept next to it as `name (git 1a2b3c4).md`.
- **It never merges binary files.** If both sides changed an image, yours stays and theirs is kept as a copy.

Cloning into a folder that already exists keeps every file that is already there. Files already there with different content are counted, not overwritten.

### Shallow clones

A clone fetches only the latest commit (depth 1). A merge needs the commit both sides share (the *merge base*), so when a pull cannot find it, Lumen deepens the clone automatically: 50, then 500, then 5,000 commits, and finally the full history.

## Public repositories need no token

Clone and pull work on public repositories without a token. You need a token (GitHub: a fine-grained personal access token with *Contents: read & write*) only for private repositories and for pushing. The token stays on this device in the encrypted secret store.

## CORS proxy

Browsers only let a page talk to servers that allow it (CORS), and GitHub, GitLab and most git hosts don't allow it for git traffic. In the browser, git therefore goes through a **CORS proxy**. The desktop app and git servers that send CORS headers don't need one.

**Lumen has no built-in proxy.** Choose one of these:

1. **Run one on this machine** (recommended):

   ```sh
   docker compose -f docker/git-proxy.yml up -d
   ```

   Then go to ⌘K → **Git: set CORS proxy…** → `http://localhost:9999`. Lumen's Content-Security-Policy already allows `localhost:9999`.

2. **A proxy your deployment hosts.** Build with `VITE_GIT_CORS_PROXY=https://git-proxy.example.com`. The build adds that origin to the CSP `connect-src`, and it becomes the default for every user. A user's own setting (option 1) still takes precedence.

The proxy is [@isomorphic-git/cors-proxy](https://github.com/isomorphic-git/cors-proxy) (MIT). It forwards only git smart-HTTP requests and stores nothing. Your token passes through it in the `Authorization` header, so only use a proxy you trust.

If a clone or pull fails before it reaches the git host, Lumen says so and points to this setting.

## Git LFS is not supported

Repositories that use [Git LFS](https://git-lfs.com) store large files as small *pointer* files, and the real content lives on a separate LFS server that Lumen does not talk to. What happens:

- A clone writes the pointer files as they are and lists them, so you know those files are not the real content.
- A pull **never replaces a real file with a pointer**. If the vault has the real file and upstream has a pointer, the file is kept and reported.
- A commit **never replaces a pointer with the real file**: the repository keeps its pointer and the commit tells you which files it kept that way, so a large file is not pushed as an ordinary Git object and the repository's LFS tracking stays intact.

To work with LFS content, check the repository out with the git command line and open that folder as your vault.

pages.title: Sync on the local network
pages.description: Sync two devices directly over your own network, end-to-end encrypted, with no cloud and no internet.
pages.md:
Next to WebDAV, S3, Dropbox and Google Drive, the [encrypted sync](/sync/e2ee/)
can keep your vault on **your local network only**. One device keeps the
vault and the others pair with it directly. There's no server, no account
and no cloud, and it works with no internet connection at all.

## Set it up

1. On the device that keeps the vault (a desktop that's usually on): ⌘K →
   *Encrypted sync…* → **Local network** → *Keeps the vault* → *Connect*,
   then choose a passphrase.
2. Still there: **Pair a device**. Lumen shows a pairing code as a QR code
   and as text.
3. On the other device: ⌘K → *Encrypted sync…* → **Local network** → *Joins
   a device that keeps the vault*. Paste or scan the code, then press *Answer*.
4. Bring the answer code back to the first device, paste it there and
   press *Connect*.
5. On the joining device, unlock the vault with the same passphrase.

From then on each device syncs **on its own**, shortly after you edit and
shortly after the other device reports a change. An edit reaches the other
device in under two seconds.

> Keep Lumen open on the device that keeps the vault while the others sync.
> If the link drops (the device slept, the network changed), pair again.
> Nothing is lost: the next round catches up.

## What crosses the network

The same thing a cloud provider would store: the vault header, plus sealed
manifests and blobs under HMAC names. The devices pass them directly, over a
WebRTC data channel (DTLS). Notes are encrypted before they leave a device
(AES-256-GCM, keys from your passphrase), exactly as with the other providers.

| | |
|---|---|
| Signaling server | None. The two pairing codes carry each device's connection details |
| STUN / TURN | None (`iceServers: []`) |
| Addresses used | Only local-network ones: 10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16, 169.254/16, 127/8, IPv6 link-local and unique-local, `*.local` |
| Who may write | Only a device that proves it knows the passphrase |

Two checks keep the link on your network:

- Every connection candidate, in both codes, must be a host candidate on
  a local-network address; any other candidate is dropped. Once connected,
  the address of the other end is checked again, and a link to anything
  outside the local network is closed.
- The device that keeps the vault serves only the vault header until the
  other device proves it knows the passphrase (an HMAC challenge in both
  directions under the vault's pairing key). A device with another
  passphrase, or one that has only a pairing code, can't list, write or
  delete anything.

The pairing codes carry no key material. The passphrase is still needed.

## The privacy ledger

Each link shows up in the privacy ledger (⌘K → *Privacy ledger*) as
*On this device / LAN*. Its host is the other device's local-network address
(or "address hidden by the browser" when the browser keeps it to itself),
along with the bytes the link carried. No entry for the LAN sync can show an
address outside your network.

## Scanning the QR code

The web app can't open the camera: its permissions policy turns the camera
off. To bring a code across, scan the QR code with another device's camera
app, or copy and paste the text, for example through a note-to-self or
AirDrop. Native scanning and automatic discovery of devices (mDNS) belong
to the desktop and mobile apps, and are not part of this version.

## How it's checked

- `src/__tests__/lanSync.test.ts`: two devices, the real sync engine, the
  link with LAN latency. **1,000 rounds** of random edits and deletions on
  both sides, sometimes at the same moment, end with **0 lost** (and every
  concurrent write kept, in the note or its conflict copy). The link
  carries no note text, and there is **not one** `fetch`. A change reaches
  the other device in **under 2 s**, both ways. Wrong passphrases and wrong
  hosts are refused.
- `e2e/lan-sync.spec.ts`: two browsers pair with the codes, unlock and sync
  both ways on their own. They make no request except to the app's own
  server, and the ledger shows local-network addresses only.

pages.title: Automatic merging
pages.description: When the same note changed in two places, Lumen merges the two edits itself and asks only when both changed the same words — the same way for encrypted sync, git and edits made outside Lumen.
pages.md:
A note can change in two places at once: on your laptop and your phone
between two syncs, in Lumen and in a `git pull`, or in Lumen and in another
editor working on the same folder. Lumen merges both edits on its own, keeps
both versions in the note's history, and opens the conflict dialog only for
the part both sides changed in different ways.

## How the merge works

Lumen compares each version with the last one both sides had:

1. **Front matter, key by key.** A field one side changed takes that change.
   When both sides changed a list — `tags`, `aliases` — both sets of
   additions and removals are applied (`[a, b]` + `c` here, `d` there →
   `[a, b, c, d]`). The same field changed to two different values is a
   conflict. The merged front matter must be valid YAML; if it would not be,
   Lumen does not merge it.
2. **The body, line by line.** Lines only one side touched take that side's
   version.
3. **Then word by word.** If both sides edited the same line or paragraph —
   one fixed a typo, the other added a word — both edits are kept.
4. **What is left asks.** Only when both sides changed the *same words*
   differently (or one deleted what the other edited) does the conflict
   dialog open, showing just those places.

Nothing is lost: both versions go into the note's **history** (marked *kept
at a merge*), so any merge can be undone from the version list.

## Where it applies

| Where | What happens |
|---|---|
| [Encrypted sync](/sync/e2ee/) | A note both devices changed is merged before the dialog; binary files are kept side by side. |
| [Git](/sync/git/) | A pull merges the files both sides changed; what still overlaps gets the usual conflict markers for the resolution screen. |
| Changes outside Lumen | A note with unsaved edits that another app changed on disk is merged into the editor and saved; if you keep typing while it merges, the dialog decides instead. |

All three use the same merge engine (`src/sync/merge/textMerge.ts`).

## How often it merges by itself

In the test of 500 random pairs of concurrent edits to ordinary notes (a
few word changes, new lines, deleted lines, new tags and changed fields on
each side), 459 merge without a dialog (92%), every word either side added
is in the result, and the front matter is valid YAML in every merge.

pages.title: Publish to your own site
pages.description: Turn the notes you pick into a website with navigation, search and right-to-left pages, on your own GitHub Pages or as a .zip for any static host.
pages.md:
`⌘K → Publish site…` turns the notes you pick into a static website that
you host yourself. Lumen runs no server for it, and the site belongs to you.

## What you get

- **A page per note**, rendered by the same pipeline as the preview and the
  HTML export: diagrams, math, tables and code.
- **Navigation** on every page: a tree of the published notes by folder, with
  the current page marked, and a link home.
- **Search** in the site bar. It runs in the visitor's browser over the site's
  own `search-index.json`, ignores case and Hebrew niqqud, and sends nothing
  anywhere.
- **Right-to-left.** A Hebrew or Arabic note is laid out right-to-left. With
  the site language set to Hebrew, the bar, navigation and search are
  right-to-left and in Hebrew too.
- **Links work.** `[[wiki links]]` and `.md` links point at the published
  pages. A link to a note you did not pick keeps its text but loses the link,
  so the site has no dead links and does not reveal where an unpublished note
  lives. Images and other files the notes reference are copied along. A file
  that cannot be found stays a plain link, and the result says how many.
- `index.md` at the vault root becomes the home page. Without one, the home
  page lists every page. A `404.html` and a `.nojekyll` are included.

## Where it goes

**A .zip file.** Download the site and put it on any static host: drag it
onto [Netlify Drop](https://app.netlify.com/drop), upload it to Cloudflare
Pages, or unpack it on a web server. Nothing leaves your device until you do.

**GitHub Pages.** Give the repository (`owner/name`, or its URL), a branch
(default `gh-pages`) and a GitHub token that may write to the repository's
contents and Pages. If you leave the token empty, the token of
[git sync](/sync/git/) is used. Publishing makes **one commit** on that branch,
on top of its previous one (no force push), so every earlier version stays in
its history. The commit holds exactly the site, so a page you unpublish is
gone from the next version. Lumen then switches Pages on for that branch and
shows the address. GitHub can take a minute before it serves a new version.

The repository needs at least one commit (a README is enough). An empty
repository is refused with that message. Only the site's files are sent, only
to `api.github.com`, and only when you press **Publish**. The token is kept on
your device.

The form remembers the site title, language, target, repository, branch and
your pick of notes.

## Not included

- Embeds (`![[note]]`) are published as written. They appear once the embed
  renderer (plan 4.7) is part of this build.
- Netlify and Cloudflare Pages deploys through their APIs (the .zip covers them
  today), and RSS.

pages.title: Read-mode publishing
pages.description: Publishing a note as a read-only web page — what exists today, the server it needs, and what is not built yet.
pages.md:
:::caution[Not in the app yet]
The publishing code exists (`src/sync/publish.ts`), but **no screen or
command calls it yet**. This page describes what is there, so a host can
set up the server side ahead of the button.
:::

## What it does

`publishNote()` sends a note to a publish server, which stores the rendered
page and answers with its public URL and slug. `unpublishNote()` makes it
private again. A note can be published as **public** or **unlisted**, and
with a password: the body is then encrypted on this device before it is
sent, so the server only ever holds ciphertext. The slug is kept in the
note's front matter (`published: <slug>`) so that publishing again updates
the same page. Publishing needs a plan with cloud features (Pro / Team).

## The server

Any HTTP endpoint that accepts the same JSON works. The reference is a
Cloudflare Worker in `edge-workers/publish`; the steps to deploy it are in
`DEPLOY.md` (section *Publish edge worker*). The app finds the server
through `VITE_PUBLISH_ENDPOINT` at build time. Without it, a development
build (or one on `localhost`) publishes into a local mock, and any other
build refuses with *“VITE_PUBLISH_ENDPOINT is not set”*.

The browser never holds a service key: requests carry the user's session.

pages.title: Sync status, selective sync and time left
pages.description: See what the encrypted sync is doing for every file, choose what each device syncs, and how long a round will take.
pages.md:
The encrypted sync (see [Encrypted sync](/sync/e2ee/)) shows its work.
Open **Sync** from the command palette (⌘K → *Encrypted sync…*) while the
vault is unlocked.

## A state for every file and folder

While the vault is unlocked, the file tree shows a small mark after each
name:

| Mark | State | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| ✓ | Synced | This device and the vault have the same version. |
| ↻ | Waiting to sync | A change waits to go up or come down in the next round. An edit shows here as soon as you save it. |
| ! | Conflict | The note was changed here and on another device, and you have not chosen what to keep yet. |
| × | Can't sync | The path can't be synced as it is, for example a file here and a folder with the same name on another device. |
| – | Not synced on this device | Left out by this device's rules (below). |

A folder shows the most urgent state inside it: error, then conflict, then
waiting. Screen readers read each mark's name.

## Activity

The **Activity** section of the Sync panel lists what the sync did: every
file sent and received, with its size, deletions, notes kept on this device
and why, and the start and end of every round. A conflict is listed **the
moment the round finds it**, while the conflict dialog is still open.
**Needs attention** lists the files in conflict, with an error, or waiting.

The list is kept on this device only and is never uploaded.

## Time left

While a round runs, the panel shows a progress bar, how many files and
bytes are done, and an estimate of the time left ("about 3 min left"). The
estimate weighs files and bytes equally: a round of many small notes is
bound by requests, one of a few videos by bandwidth. Before anything has
finished it uses the speed of this device's earlier rounds; on the very
first round it says "estimating time left…" until it can measure.

## Selective sync: what this device syncs

Under **What syncs on this device** you can leave out:

- **folders** (one per line, e.g. `Videos` or `Archive/2019`), with everything inside;
- **file types** (e.g. `mp4, mov`);
- **attachments over a size** in MB. Notes (`.md`, `.txt`, …) are never left out for their size.

The rules are **per device** and saved **on this device only**. A phone can
skip `Videos/` while the laptop syncs everything. The form is shown before
you unlock too, so you can set the rules before a device's first round.

A file that is left out is invisible to the sync in both directions:

- it is **never read for upload and never leaves the device**, not even
  encrypted, and the vault's manifest does not name it;
- a newer version from another device is **not downloaded**, and a
  deletion made elsewhere is **not applied** here.

If the saved rules can't be read (damaged browser storage), the sync stops
with a message instead of syncing everything. Save the rules again to
continue.

## In the background (iOS, Android, browsers)

Lumen syncs when it goes to the background and when it comes back, and
every 5 minutes while it is open. iOS and Android pause apps in the
background, and a browser tab that is not visible may be paused too, so
sync does not run while Lumen is closed. The vault's keys exist only in
memory, and keeping them on the device so that a system task could sync
would weaken the encryption. When you come back after more than two
minutes and no round ran in between, the panel says so ("Sync did not run
while Lumen was in the background…") and a round starts at once.

## Benchmark

`npm run bench:sync` syncs 10,000 notes and 1 GB of attachments through a
local WebDAV server: device A's first sync up, device B's first sync down,
then one changed note each way. Plan limits: under 10 minutes for a first
sync, under 3 seconds for a single change.

pages.title: Sync in two clicks
pages.description: A guided setup that picks the best place for your encrypted notes on this device, makes the key for you, and shows every file's state.
pages.md:
Run **Set up sync (two clicks)** from the command palette.

## 1. Where the encrypted copy lives

The best choice for this device is already selected:

| Place | When it is first | What you need |
|---|---|---|
| **A folder of iCloud Drive, Dropbox, Google Drive or OneDrive** | On a computer whose browser can open folders (Chrome, Edge) | The sync app you already have. Lumen writes only encrypted files, into a `Lumen sync` folder inside the one you pick. |
| **Lumen's encrypted relay** | On phones, and browsers that can't open folders | Nothing. The relay stores encrypted files and can't read them. |
| **WebDAV** (Nextcloud, a NAS) | When neither of the above is there | The server's address, user name and password. |

**Advanced** opens the full panel: S3, and Dropbox or Google Drive through
their own sign-in once those are available.

## 2. Your key: 13 Hebrew words

Lumen makes the key for you: 12 random words from a list of 256 everyday
Hebrew words (96 bits), and a 13th word that checks the others, so a typo
is caught at once. Write them down or keep them in a password manager, then
type back the word Lumen asks for. That shows you saved them.

**Before anything starts, the setup says it plainly:** without these words
nobody can open the encrypted copy, not even Lumen. Your notes on the device
stay either way.

## 3. Every file's state

After the first round the setup lists how many files are **synced**,
**waiting**, in **conflict**, or **can't sync**, and names each one that
needs you. The file tree shows the same state next to every note
([Sync status](/sync/status/)).

## The next device

Open Lumen, run **Set up sync**, choose the same place, tap **I already have
a key**, and paste the 13 words. Typing is forgiving: niqqud, punctuation,
extra spaces and final letters (ם or מ) don't matter.

## How the relay keeps no secrets

The relay sees a token that is a hash of your words, never the words, and
stores only a hash of that token. Every object it keeps was encrypted on
your device with keys it never sees (the [encrypted sync](/sync/e2ee/)
format). It deletes a space nobody has read or written for 180 days: a vault
you only read on your devices is kept.

Running your own relay: `VAULT_RELAY=1 node sync-server/server.js` (or
`node sync-server/vault-relay.js`), with `VAULT_RELAY_DIR` to keep the
objects on disk, and build the app with `VITE_SYNC_RELAY_URL` set to its
https address.

A token costs nothing to make, so the relay also limits what one address and
the whole server can hold:

| Setting | Default | What it limits |
|---|---|---|
| `VAULT_RELAY_MAX_SPACE` | 1 GiB | one vault's space |
| `VAULT_RELAY_MAX_TOTAL` | 20 GiB | all spaces together |
| `VAULT_RELAY_NEW_SPACES_PER_DAY` | 5 | new spaces one address may open a day |
| `VAULT_RELAY_ADDRESS_BYTES_PER_DAY` | the space size | bytes one address may write a day |

Addresses are never stored: the relay counts them under a keyed hash whose
key is random, kept in memory only and replaced every day.

An IPv6 address counts as its /64, since one host usually holds a whole /64.
The counts sit in a fixed-size table that never forgets an address, so other
addresses cannot reset them. A burst of requests sent at once is counted in
full. Every object is charged the disk space it takes, in whole 4 KiB blocks,
so many tiny objects cost what they really cost.

Behind a reverse proxy, every request comes from the proxy's address. Mounted
in `server.js`, the relay uses the client address that `server.js` reads
(`SIGNAL_TRUST_PROXY=1`, which `fly.toml` sets): `Fly-Client-IP` only on Fly,
and otherwise the last `X-Forwarded-For` entry, the one the proxy in front
added. The standalone relay trusts no header unless you tell it to, because
on a shared network (a school, an office) any machine could otherwise name
any address it liked:

| `VAULT_RELAY_TRUST_PROXY` | The client address is |
|---|---|
| not set | on Fly, as `fly`; anywhere else, the connection's own address |
| `0` | the connection's own address |
| `fly` | `Fly-Client-IP`, only on Fly and only from Fly's proxy |
| a list of the proxies' own addresses, e.g. `10.0.0.2/32,fd00::2/128` | the connections from those proxies: the right-most `X-Forwarded-For` entry that is not one of them. When every entry is a proxy, the connection's own address. A range wider than /24 (IPv4) or /64 (IPv6) would hold clients too, so the relay ignores it |

An IPv6 client counts as its /64 for every limit. For new spaces, its /48
counts as well (`VAULT_RELAY_NEW_SPACES_PER_48`, 16 times the per-address
limit by default), so one tunnel's many /64s are not many clients.

A public relay can also ask for more before it opens a new space (existing
spaces are not affected):

- `VAULT_RELAY_POW_BITS=18`: a proof of work. The app solves it by itself, in
  a few seconds, the first time it writes to a new space. The relay accepts
  at most 24 bits, the most the app will solve.
- `VAULT_RELAY_INVITE=<secret>`: an invite. Build the app with
  `VITE_SYNC_RELAY_INVITE` set to the same secret. Anyone who has the build has
  the invite, so use it for a relay whose app you don't publish.

pages.title: Academic submission (Word)
pages.description: Export a note as a Word file formatted to an Israeli university's written guideline, with a title page, a table of contents, page numbers, footnotes and a bibliography.
pages.md:
Students write in Lumen and submit in Word. **Export for academic submission**
turns a note into a `.docx` that follows one institution's published
formatting guideline, so you don't have to fix it by hand.

## Export

`⌘K → Export for academic submission (Word)…`

1. Pick the **institution**. The line under it shows the font, size, spacing
   and margins it uses, with a link to the guideline they come from.
2. Check the **title page** fields. They start from the note's frontmatter.
3. Choose whether to add a **table of contents**, and how its page is
   numbered: no number, Hebrew letters (א, ב, ג) or Roman numerals.
4. Press **Export .docx**. Open the file in Word and press **F9** on the table
   of contents to fill in the page numbers. Word also offers to do this when
   it opens the file.

## What the file contains

- **Title page** (not numbered): the institution, faculty and department, the
  title, the kind of work, the course and its number, the lecturer, and at the
  foot of the page your name, ID number and the submission date.
- **Table of contents**: Word's own table of contents over headings 1–3, with
  links to the chapters.
- **Body**: numbered from 1 in the footer. Each top-level heading (`#`)
  starts a new page where the guideline asks for it.
- **Footnotes**: Markdown footnotes (`text[^1]` with `[^1]: the note`) become
  real Word footnotes, single-spaced and smaller, each one right-to-left or
  left-to-right by its own text.
- **Bibliography**: a heading named *Bibliography*, *References*,
  *ביבליוגרפיה*, *רשימת מקורות* or *מקורות* starts on a new page, and the
  entries under it get a hanging indent without bullets or numbers.

## Title page from the frontmatter

```yaml
---
title: Digital tools in Hebrew academic writing
subtitle: Seminar paper
faculty: Faculty of Social Sciences
department: Department of Education
course: Seminar in writing research
course_number: 12-345
lecturer: Dr. Ronit Cohen
author: Israel Israeli
student_id: "012345678"
date: March 2026
institution: biu
---
```

Hebrew keys work too: `כותרת`, `סוג העבודה`, `פקולטה`, `חוג`, `קורס`,
`מספר קורס`, `מרצה`, `מגיש`, `ת״ז`, `תאריך`, `מוסד`. The title page's labels
follow the note's language, not the app's.

## The institutions

| Institution | Covers | Font, size, spacing | Margins (right / left / top / bottom) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| The Hebrew University (`huji`) | Humanities papers | David 11, double, justified | 2.54 cm (Word's default; the guideline says only not to reduce them) |
| Bar-Ilan University (`biu`) | Seminar papers | David 12, 1.5 | 2.5 cm |
| University of Haifa (`haifa`) | Master's thesis, social work | David 12, 1.5 | 3 / 2 / 2 / 2 cm |
| The Open University (`openu`) | Master's thesis, history | David 12, 1.5, front matter in Roman numerals | 3 / 2 / 2 / 2 cm |
| Tel Aviv University (`tau`) | Master's thesis, medicine | 12, 1.5 (David, 2.5 cm margins where the guideline is silent) | 2.5 cm |

Departments often have their own rules. Check yours before you submit.
Latin text uses Times New Roman throughout.

pages.title: Fill properties with AI — with approval
pages.description: A model proposes the missing properties of a folder's notes; every proposal waits in an approval queue, and nothing is written until you approve it.
pages.md:
`⌘K → "AI: Fill Properties for Notes…"` asks for a folder (empty for the
whole workspace) and proposes values for the **properties your notes
already use** — the frontmatter fields that appear in at least two notes.

## How it works

1. **The fields.** Each property's type comes from the values it has in
   the vault (text, number, date, list, checkbox, link). When a property
   uses only a few values (up to 12, like `status: draft / done`), the
   model must pick one of them.
2. **The answer is constrained.** The `autofiller` agent answers with JSON
   that must match a JSON Schema built for the request: only those
   properties, each with its type and allowed values. An answer that
   doesn't match is sent back once with the reason; a note whose answer
   still fails is skipped.
3. **Only missing values.** A property the note already has is kept; only
   missing or empty ones are proposed.
4. **The approval queue.** Each note's proposal shows every property's
   *before → after*. **Approve** writes that note, **Approve all** writes
   every one, **Reject** drops it. Nothing is written before that. The
   write changes only the proposed values — comments, order and quoting in
   the frontmatter stay byte for byte — and a note that changed after the
   proposal is not written.

Notes open in a tab are left out (they may have unsaved edits). The agent
runs through the agent runtime, so under the *local only* policy on a local
model.

pages.title: Automations (when… then…)
pages.description: Simple rules that file, tag and log your notes on this device — with a dry run that changes nothing, a log of every run, and undo.
pages.md:
An automation is a rule: **when** something happens to a note, **then**
Lumen does something. Rules run on this device only; nothing is sent
anywhere.

| When… | Then… |
|---|---|
| a note is created (anywhere, or in a folder) | move it to a folder |
| a tag is added (in the frontmatter or as `#tag`) | add a tag |
| a property changes (to any value, or to one value) | apply a template (its text, and frontmatter keys the note does not have) |
| every day (once a day) | add a line to today's daily note (`{{link}}`, `{{title}}`, `{{date}}`) |

## Make a rule

Command palette → **Automations: new rule (when… then…)…**: pick the
trigger, then the action, and answer one question for each (the folder,
the tag, the property…). The rules are kept in `.lumen/automations.json`
in the vault, which you can also edit by hand.

## Dry run

**Automations: dry run on this note** shows what the rules would do to the
open note as if it had just been created — which rules, which files —
without writing anything.

## Undo

Every run is logged in `.lumen/automations-log.json` with the text of each
file before and after. **Automations: undo the last run** puts every file
back byte for byte, and moves moved notes back. When a file was edited by
hand after the run, undo stops and says which file, instead of overwriting
your edit.

## No loops

A rule's own changes can trigger other rules (tag → move → the move's
"created in Done" → tag), but a rule runs at most once per note in one
chain, and a chain stops after three steps. Two rules that would bounce a
note between folders forever stop after one round. A line added to the
daily note triggers nothing.

## How it was checked

`src/__tests__/automations.test.ts`: 20 golden rules, each run on a small
vault: the dry run writes nothing, the run gives exactly the expected
files, and undo gives back every byte; plus the loop guard, undo refusing
over a later edit, tags, the rules file and once-a-day.

pages.title: Backups to a second drive
pages.description: A daily backup of the whole vault to another drive or folder, plain or encrypted with age, kept 7 days, 4 weeks and 6 months, and a restore you can check.
pages.md:
Version history protects you from your own edits, but it lives on the same
disk as the vault. **Backups** copy the whole vault somewhere else, once a
day while Lumen is open.

## Set it up

⌘K → *Backups…*, then choose one of:

- **Back up to a folder or drive…** writes a plain `.tar` archive that any
  archive tool opens.
- **Back up encrypted to a folder or drive…** writes `.tar.age`, encrypted
  with [age](https://age-encryption.org) to a backup key made for you. The
  panel shows the key (`AGE-SECRET-KEY-1…`) once. Keep it away from this
  device: without it nobody can open the backup, you included. Only its
  public half is stored.

A folder that is the vault, or inside it, is refused: backups there would
sync, and every backup would contain the ones before it. Git internals and
the trash aren't backed up.

## What's kept

The newest backup of each of the last **7 days**, **4 weeks** and **6
months**: at most 17 archives. Older ones are deleted after each backup.

## When something's wrong

- A backup that fails (an unplugged drive, a folder the browser no longer
  lets Lumen write to) is shown at once: a notice, and a red line in the
  panel. Lumen tries again after 15 minutes.
- **Three days** without a successful backup is shown once a day.

## Restore

- **Restore everything to a new folder…** puts the newest backup's files
  into a folder you pick.
- **Restore it into the vault** restores one file or folder. Nothing is
  overwritten: a file that's already there is restored next to it, as
  `name (restored 2026-11-10).md`.

Every archive starts with a list of its files and their SHA-256. A restore
checks each file and refuses a damaged archive.

Without Lumen:

```sh
tar -xf lumen-backup-2026-11-10T03-12-00Z.tar
age -d -i backup-key.txt lumen-backup-….tar.age | tar -x
```

## How it's checked

`src/__tests__/backup.test.ts` backs up 1,000 notes and 200 attachments,
deletes the vault and restores it, plain and encrypted: **every file has the
same SHA-256**. It also checks that a broken drive is reported within a
minute, and that a backup writes nothing into the vault.
`e2e/backup-drill.spec.ts` runs the same drill from the panel in the browser.

## Limits

- The browser needs the File System Access API to write to a folder
  (Chromium). The desktop app's own folder access (Tauri) and WebDAV targets
  are behind the same `BackupTarget` interface and come with their pull
  requests.
- Backups run while Lumen is open, so a laptop that's always closed gets
  none. The three-day notice says so.

pages.title: Writing a book
pages.description: Chapters as notes in order, word goals per chapter and per book, today's words and a streak, and the book assembled into a Hebrew EPUB 3 and a print-ready PDF.
pages.md:
A book in Lumen is a folder of notes, one per chapter, and an **index
note** that lists the chapters in order. The index uses the format of
Obsidian's [Longform](https://github.com/kevboh/longform) plugin, so the
same book opens in Obsidian too.

## Start a book

Open any note in the folder and run **Book: chapters, goals and export**
from the command palette (`⌘K` / `Ctrl+K`). When the note is not in a book
yet, Lumen offers to make one: it asks for the title and writes an index
note whose chapters are the folder's notes, in name order (`01`, `02`, …
sort as numbers). **Book: add this note as a chapter** adds the open note to
the end of the book whose index is in the same folder.

The index note looks like this:

```yaml
---
longform:
  format: scenes
  title: The Orchard
  sceneFolder: /
  scenes:
    - Opening
    - - A scene inside the opening   # a nested list: parts of a chapter
    - The second chapter
word-goal: 80000   # the book's goal
daily-goal: 500    # words a day, for the streak
author: Noa Cohen
lang: he
---
```

A chapter's own goal is `word-goal:` in the chapter's frontmatter.
Lumen's keys sit outside `longform:`, which Longform rewrites.

## The book panel

The panel lists the chapters in order with their word counts and goals,
the book's total against its goal, the words written today and the
streak (days in a row on which the daily goal was met). Drag a chapter,
or use its ↑ ↓ buttons, to reorder; only the `scenes:` list in the index
changes. A nested part moves with its chapter. Click a chapter to open it.

Today's words are the book's total now minus its total at the end of the
last day you wrote, so deleting counts against the day. The totals are
kept in a small hidden file next to the index
(`.<index name>.lumen-book.json`, which Obsidian does not show).

### How words are counted

Only prose counts: frontmatter, code, comments (`%% … %%`), link targets,
embeds and Markdown marks do not. A Hebrew word with its prefixes is one
word, also when a hyphen or maqaf joins the prefix to a number or a Latin
word (`ה-CNN`, `ב־1948`); abbreviations with geresh or gershayim (`צה״ל`,
`מס׳`) and maqaf compounds (`בית־ספר`) are one word each. A spaced dash is
not a word.

## EPUB

**Export EPUB** writes `<title>.epub`: a title page, a table of contents,
one file per chapter, the book's font (Frank Ruhl Libre, SIL Open Font
Licence) and the images the chapters show. A Hebrew book opens from the
right in Apple Books, Kindle and other readers
(`page-progression-direction="rtl"`, `dir="rtl"` and `lang="he"` on every
page); an English chapter inside it reads left to right. Links to other
notes become plain text (they lead nowhere in a book); links to the web
stay. The book keeps the same identifier across exports, so a reader keeps
your place and highlights.

## Print and PDF

**Print / PDF** opens the book in a print window; choose **Save as PDF**
in the print dialog. Pages are A5 with the chapter title on a new page,
page numbers at the bottom (none on the title and contents pages), the
paragraph indent of a printed book and Hebrew right to left.

## How it was checked

- `src/__tests__/bookMode.test.ts`: the word count rules, the index (read,
  reorder, add, comments and CRLF kept), progress, the streak, and a
  30-chapter book counted in well under 10 seconds.
- `src/__tests__/bookEpub.test.ts`: the package structure (stored
  `mimetype` first, RTL spine, navigation, font, images), well-formed XHTML
  chapters, 30 chapters assembled in well under 10 seconds, and the print
  document.
- A 30-chapter Hebrew book with footnotes, a table, code and an English
  chapter, assembled in a browser (0.3 s): **epubcheck 5.3.0 — 0 errors,
  0 warnings**; its PDF has 62 A5 pages with Frank Ruhl Libre embedded.

Not yet checked by hand: opening the EPUB in Apple Books and Kindle
Previewer.
